summary: Retires the MD2 message digest algorithm and discusses why, moving RFC 1319 to Historic status. It is informational.

eli5.summary: MD2 is an old way to make a fingerprint of data. Because it is weak, this note says to stop using it.

subtitle: Why the MD2 hash algorithm was retired and RFC 1319 moved to Historic status.

tldr.problem: MD2, published in 1992, has since been shown to fall short of the properties a hash needs, yet some RFCs still referred to it.
tldr.mechanism: The document reviews the attacks on MD2, lists the RFCs that mention it and the minimal impact on each, and moves RFC 1319 to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: MD2 should not be used for digital signatures and should be replaced by an existing hash algorithm such as SHA-256.

today: RFC 6149 moves RFC 1319 to Historic status and is itself Informational, with no later RFC obsoleting or updating it in the unit metadata. It recommends SHA-256 or another existing hash algorithm instead of MD2.

sections.title: Retiring MD2
sections.content: MD2 is a message digest algorithm. It takes a message of arbitrary length and produces a 128-bit "fingerprint" or "message digest" of the input. RFC 6149 retires it by moving RFC 1319 to Historic status and explains why. It assumes the reader knows RFC 4270, which summarizes how attacks on a hash's one-way and collision-free properties affect Internet protocols.
sections.eli5: MD2 squeezes any file down to a short fingerprint. This note says it is time to stop using that recipe.

sections.title: Why MD2 Is Retired
sections.content:
MD2 was published in 1992 as an Informational RFC. Since then it has been shown not to be collision-free, although the document admits that successful collision attacks on a properly implemented MD2 are not that damaging. Successful pre-image and second pre-image attacks have also been shown.

The document adds a practical point: MD2 has fallen out of favor because it is slower than MD4 and MD5, since it was optimized for 8-bit machines while those two were optimized for 32-bit machines. It is also slower than the SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 algorithms of the Secure Hash Standard.
sections.eli5: People found tricks to break MD2's fingerprints, and it is also slow on modern computers.

sections.title: Who Still Referred to MD2
sections.content:
The RFC lists documents that specify MD2: RFC 3279 and RFC 4572 (Proposed Standards), several Informational RFCs (RFC 1983, 2315, 2898 and 3447), and the Experimental RFC 2660. It also notes RFC 2313 and RFC 2437 as exceptions to its omission of older documents.

The impact of the move is described as minimal. MD2 support in TLS was dropped in TLS 1.1. MD2 is optional in RFC 4572, where SHA-1 is the preferred algorithm. RFC 3279 keeps it for compatibility with older applications, but its use is discouraged. RFC 2660 was largely supplanted by RFC 2818, "HTTP Over TLS", and is the only RFC found that references HMAC-MD2.
sections.eli5: A few old documents mentioned MD2, but most had already moved on, so taking MD2 off the shelf breaks very little.

sections.title: What the Attacks Show
sections.content:
MD2 is not a straight Merkle-Damgaard design: for a padded message with t blocks it computes a nonlinear checksum as block t+1. Its collision resistance depends heavily on that checksum. Without it, a collision can be found in 2^12 MD2 operations. With it, the best collision attack takes 2^63.3 operations with 2^50 memory, not significantly better than the birthday attack.

The bigger problem is that MD2 is not one-way. A pre-image can be found with 2^104 MD2 operations, and an improved attack needs 2^73. A pre-image attack can also yield a second pre-image, which is more severe for digital signatures than a collision attack, so MD2 must not be used for digital signatures. Because it is "invertible", using it in HMAC may also leak information about keys.
sections.eli5: Finding two files with the same fingerprint is hard, but working backwards from a fingerprint to a file is much easier than it should be. That makes it unsafe for signing.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
Even though MD2 saw some deployment on the Internet, the document recommends obsoleting it. MD2 is not a reasonable candidate for further standardization and should be deprecated in favor of existing hash algorithms such as SHA-256. It notes that RSA Security considers it appropriate to move MD2 to Historic status.

The reasoning is that deploying and withdrawing cryptography each take years, so algorithms need to be withdrawn before a catastrophic break is found. Implementations should strongly consider removing support and migrating to another hash algorithm.
sections.eli5: Take away old locks before a burglar proves they can be picked, because swapping them takes a long time.
